Good evening, everyone. So the Water Day was led by the Deputy Prime Minister's Office. Deputy Prime Minister Namtba Bayar, but the office sends their apologies for not being able to come here. So they asked me to read the closing remarks on their behalf. So excellencies, distinguished delegates, and ladies and gentlemen, drought is becoming more frequent, more severe, and more destructive. It threatens water and food supplies, damages ecosystems, destroys livelihood, and increases inequality and instability. The message from the water day at COP17 is clear. Drought is not a temporary emergency. It is a global economic, environmental and security risk. And that is why the government of Mongolia launched two global initiatives on water land nexus initiative and nature based solutions for sustainable infrastructure initiative as part of the step action agenda and water day brought together voices from across the world. Beyond the ministerial dialogue, 15 high level events, 34 side events were held in the blue zone and also 32 side events in the green zone. All of these side events were the truly whole of society approach based. And all of these events expanded participation and created space for technical policy, community level discussions on drought resilience, water security, land restoration, finance, governance, and locally led solutions. And from all of these discussions, several priorities emerged. First, we must move from reaction to anticipation. Droughts and floods are not unexpected events. They are recurring risks. We must manage them through national plans, early warning systems, prearranged funding and finance that is really released when agreed risk thresholds are reached. Second, water is the connector. Land degradation and desertification are also water management challenges. Healthy land holds water. Healthy ecosystems protect communities. Wetlands, peatlands, rangelands, and watersheds support water security and resilience. Moreover, deep groundwater that cannot be naturally renewed must be strictly protected. Once it is lost, it may be lost forever. Third, finance remains the greatest constraint. Countries need strong bankable project pipelines. They need more concessional and blended capital, country-led investment plans, and simpler access to funding. Drought resilience must be recognized as an investable asset. It protects food systems, economies, communities, and peace. We already know that well-designed investment can mobilize resources at scale. For example, the Jeff seven dry land sustainable landscape program used 104 million US dollars to leverage more than $800 million across 11 countries. And this shows what is possible when public finance partnership and clear national priorities come together. Fourth, nature-based solutions must move beyond small standalone projects. Restoring wetlands, peatlands, range lands and watersheds can reduce drought risk and strengthen water security. But these solutions must be supported by evidence. Their value and cost effectiveness must be demonstrated in the field. They must then be built into infrastructure planning, regulations and local laws, not treated as temporary pilot projects. Fifth, local communities must be recognized as implementers. Women, Young people, indigenous people, farmers, pastoralists, and local communities are not simply beneficiaries. They are leaders, knowledge holders, and entrepreneurs. Yet funding often fails to reach them. We must address the barriers created by short-term project funding, collateral requirements, and insecure land tenure. Resilience will remain an idea unless resources reach the people who deliver it on the ground. And finally, strong governance and cooperation are essential. Drought does not respect national borders. Shared rivers, aquifers, ecosystems, and sand and dust storms require shared solutions. Discussions during the Water Day highlighted the need for stronger restoration of laws, protection of river banks, riparian zones, science-based cooperation of a transboundary water, and regional action on shared basins. They also considered the possibility of possible legally binding global drought protocol. Whatever form the final outcome takes, it must strengthen accountability while providing countries with finance, technology, capacity needed to act. So the choice before us is simple. We can continue paying the rising cost of disaster or we can invest in prevention. We can wait until wells run dry, harvests fail, and families lose their livelihoods, or we can act now. Let us move from reaction to anticipation. Let us protect water by restoring land. Let us finance resilience before disaster strikes, and let us ensure that solutions reach every country and every community. Thank you.
